c.tagline: One Happy Island — Dutch-colonial color, cactus deserts, and blinding-white beaches.

taxi.fareNote: Aruba has no Uber or ride-hailing; taxis are unmetered with government-set fixed rates by zone — confirm the fare before departing. Cabs wait at hotels, the airport, and downtown, or can be booked by phone.

emergency.note: 911 is the general emergency line for ambulance and fire, and 100 reaches the police; US dollars and English are widely used, and emergency operators speak English.

english.label: Easy to get by in English

hood_landmark.Downtown Oranjestad: Caya G.F. Betico Croes Oranjestad colorful buildings

avoid.reason: Petty theft from rental cars and unattended beach bags is the main risk — never leave valuables in sight.

hood_desc: The colorful Dutch-colonial capital, where pastel gabled facades line Caya G.F. Betico Croes, the cruise terminal, and the free streetcar; the walkable base for shopping, dining, and history.
Aruba's glittering high-rise strip, packed with beachfront resorts, casinos, rooftop bars, restaurants, and the island's liveliest nightlife along a wide white-sand beach.
A calmer low-rise resort stretch along one of the Caribbean's widest, most photographed beaches, framed by the iconic fofoti trees; ideal for a relaxed, romantic stay.
The inland district behind Palm Beach, a hub of restaurants, supermarkets, and easy access to the Alto Vista Chapel and California Lighthouse; a convenient, local-feeling base near the action.

The upscale northwestern tip of calm, clear coves — Malmok, Arashi, and Boca Catalina — prized for snorkeling, the Antilla shipwreck, and quiet villas away from the resort crowds; best for a serene, water-focused stay.

water.note: Desalinated tap water is excellent and safe to drink.

transit.hours: Arubus runs roughly 6:00 AM to about 9:00-11:00 PM (later on the Palm Beach-Oranjestad corridor), with reduced Sunday and holiday service; the free downtown streetcar runs daytime hours only.
transit.note: Public transit centers on Arubus, the island bus network linking Oranjestad with Palm Beach, Eagle Beach, and San Nicolas, plus a free vintage streetcar (tram) looping through downtown Oranjestad; most visitors also use taxis or rental cars.
transit.pay: Pay the Arubus driver in cash (about Afl. 2.60 / US$2.60 one-way, or buy a smart card at the Oranjestad terminal); US dollars are accepted. The downtown streetcar is free.

car.idp: Not required (US, Canadian, and most licenses valid up to 3 months)

ferry: Renaissance Marina water taxi to Renaissance Private Island

transit.m: Arubus Airport route to Oranjestad (~20 min)
Taxi to Oranjestad (10 min, fixed fare)
Taxi to Palm Beach (20 min, fixed fare)

tip.r: A 15% service charge is often added to hotel and restaurant bills; if it isn't, 15-20% is standard, and tipping taxis and housekeeping is appreciated.

landmarks: Fort Zoutman & Willem III Tower
Aruba's oldest building, a 1798 Dutch bastion with its landmark clock tower, hosts the weekly Bon Bini folklore festival in its sun-baked courtyard.
Eagle Beach
Regularly ranked among the world's finest beaches, this blinding-white strand is famous for its sculptural fofoti trees leaning photogenically toward turquoise water.
Arikok National Park
Covering nearly a fifth of the island, this desert preserve of cacti, caves and crashing coasts shelters Conchi, Aruba's wave-splashed natural pool.
California Lighthouse
A 1916 stone lighthouse on Aruba's breezy northwest tip, named for a shipwrecked steamer, offering golden-hour views over dunes and the island's wild coastline.
Alto Vista Chapel
A tiny mustard-yellow chapel of 1750 origins standing alone amid cacti on the north coast, the peaceful birthplace of Catholicism on Aruba.
Casibari Rock Formations
Mysterious monolithic tonalite boulders rising from the cunucu scrubland, with carved steps leading to a summit platform surveying Aruba's cactus-studded interior toward Hooiberg hill.
Ayo Rock Formations
A dramatic cluster of house-sized boulders once sacred to the Caquetío people, whose reddish-brown pictographs still decorate the sheltered rock faces.
Flamingo Beach (Renaissance Island)
A private-island beach minutes from downtown by water taxi, world-famous for the resident pink flamingos that strut fearlessly among sunbathers on the sand.
National Archaeological Museum Aruba
Housed in the restored Ecury family complex downtown, this free museum traces five thousand years of indigenous Caquetío culture through ceramics, burial urns and interactive exhibits.
Caya G. F. Betico Croes (Main Street)
Oranjestad's candy-colored main shopping street, where pastel Dutch-Caribbean colonial facades and a free streetcar line make the capital's downtown irresistibly photogenic.

train.note: Aruba has no railway. The island's only rail-like service is the free streetcar loop through downtown Oranjestad, which is a short tourist tram rather than transport. Arrive by air into Queen Beatrix International Airport or by cruise ship.

bus.note: No international coach routes exist on an island. Arubus (https://www.arubus.com/) runs the island network from the Oranjestad terminal to Palm Beach, Eagle Beach, San Nicolas and the airport, roughly every 15-40 minutes depending on the route. Fares are paid in cash on board or with a Smartcard.

ferry.note: There is no scheduled passenger ferry from Aruba - the long-discussed link to Curaçao and Bonaire has never settled into a regular service, so travel between the ABC islands is by air. Oranjestad's harbour is a busy cruise terminal, and small boats run to De Palm Island and snorkelling sites as excursions.

full.name: Curaçao
full.blurb: Willemstad's pastel Dutch colonial waterfront is reached by a roughly thirty-minute flight between the ABC islands.

full.name: Bonaire
full.blurb: Protected coral reefs and pink salt flats lie a short inter-island flight away from Aruba.
